Mr. A. N. SMITH (Stormont) moved the second reading of Bill No. 71, to incorporate the St. Lawrence River Bridge Company.
Explain.

The object of
this bill is to incorporate a company to build a bridge a little above Brockville across to Morristown, New York. Last year there was before the house a bill similar to Bill No. 70, to incorporate a company to build a bridge at Gananoque. That bill has been brought up again this year. The Department of Railways and Canals objected last year to that bridge and I do not know what their present attitude is. As I say, the bill I am promoting is for a bridge between Brockville and Morristown. There is no vehicular bridge across the St. Lawrence river between Montreal and Niagara Falls, a distance of over four hundred miles.

In the last two years we have had a veritable epidemic of proposed bridges across international waters. I am not opposing this bill. I should like to make it perfectly clear that the fact that, in regard to a bill of this character, one takes the stand that there are involved conditions affecting the public interest, is no reason for anyone to say that we are opposing the bill as a private bill. But I think, in view of the large number of structures of this kind that are being proposed, there should be some declaration of public policy on the part of the government regarding matters of this nature. These bridges are proposed to be built across international waterways, yet last year and this we are giving seven or eight private companies very wide powers in regard to these matters and we are creating more bridges and establishing conditions which it will be very difficult for parliament to deal with later on.
Another point is this. These bills in my judgment have been in error sent to the private bills committee. Again I am drawing attention to this as a matter of procedure and not as a matter of criticism of the private bills committee. This bill and similar ones ought to go to the railway committee. They have to do with transportation and traffic; they have to do with the Railway Act; the Railway Act is invoked in some of them. I do not know whether it is invoked in this particular bill. Expropriation procedure under the Railway Act has been invoked and

Niagara Falls Memorial Bridge
to my mind these bills should go to the railway committee. Furthermore the government should be prepared to declare before the committee and parliament what its policy is in regard to bridges across international waterways.

I should like to inquire from the promoter of this bill whether a similar bill for the United States portion of this bridge has been before the New York state legislature. That legislature, I understand, has now risen, and if that bill has not been passed there, what object is there in pressing this bill? What disposition has been made of the bill before the New York state legislature?

This is for a
bridge across navigable waters and is dealt with by the United States congress, rather than the state authorities. A similar bill is before the United States congress at the present time.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the select standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

Before the preamble
carries, I wish again to emphasize what I said a moment ago in regard to another bill. There seems to be a good deal of misunderstanding on both sides of the house' regarding the objections that have been raised to this and other similar bills. I want to make clear that it is not a question of objecting to this as a private bill, or objecting to those who are asking incorporation as a private company. That is not the point at all. The point at issue is that the work suggested in this bill is a very important work over international waters. Up until last year or very recently there have been comparatively few of these bridges 'built, and it is not sufficient to say, because years ago we allowed private companies to build bridges, that therefore we as representatives of the public should pay no more attention to it and let any company that desires to build a bridge do so. The very presence of this and a number of other similar bills indicates to us, if we are at all thoughtful, that the time has come when the whole question of spanning these international waters should occupy the attention of parliament, and some definite policy should be determined upon and adopted by parliament. The responsibility for doing that rests at the moment with the government. I am not saying this in criticism of the government; I am merely pointing out a condition which has arisen, and indicating what to my mind and to the minds of a great many others is the duty of parliament, and ineidently at the moment the duty of the government as the leaders of the house, namely, to make some investigation and some determination of what the public policy of Canada is to be on the question of bridges crossing international waters. For instance, some of these waters are navigable. In this particular case I do not think the waters at this point are navigable, and the bridge probably will be so high that it will be clear of all navigation. But there are other waters that are navigable, and underneath the bridges over these1 waters will have to pass all the lakes traffic. This is a stupendous responsibility that we are taking at the present time in allowing bridges to be built across international waters on which passes the whole traffic of the great lakes, and we are doing it, as we also did it last year-I say this with all respect-rather lightly and rather frivolously. I know that my utterances the other day were misunderstood. It was thought per-

Niagara Falls Memorial Bridge
haps that I had some prejudice against this bill or against the member introducing it. But there is no such thing. I have nothing but the kindliest feelings towards the sponsor of this bill, as I have towards the sponsors of other bills that are introduced into this house. My point is that we are dealing here, through the medium of private bills and private companies, with something that should be a subject of public policy.
May I ask why this bridge is to be called the memorial bridge?

I explained that the other
evening and also before the committee. It is called "memorial" because of the hundred years of peace between the United States and Canada, and also in view of the jubilee year of confederation which has just passed.

I just want to put myself in the same category with reference to this bill as my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre, who has just spoken. It appears to me that the government of this country should take some stand regarding matters of this kind. Before I sit down I intend to show what the attitude of the state of New York is on similar proposals. When this bill was before the committee on the last occasion, the hon. member for Welland (Mr. Pettit) told us that so far as he was advised, the counterpart of this bill in the United States had not been defeated. I can tell him now that that bill has gone where lots of good coloured people go; it has gone to limbo. We are proposing to pass in this house a bill that is opposed by the state of New York, is opposed by the province of Ontario, is opposed by the parks commission on the Canadian side, and opposed by the state reservation commission on the other side. I do not think we will get anywhere with this bill. I just want to put before the house and before the committee a statement from the governor of the state of New York in reference to bridges, not only at Niagara, but also on the St. Lawrence. The committee will see that the state of New York has a policy on this question. I shall not read the whole of it, but just a couple of sentences.
Read it all.

Oh no, there will be
enough time taken up without my reading it all, and if I read it all it would not be good reading for those people who are always calling out "Carried!" That is for my hon friend. On March 31, 1927, Governor Smith of New York state declared:
I think the time is past when the state should incorporate companies of this kind
Such bridges should be built either from public funds or through an agency such as the port authority of New York, authorized to issue bonds at a low rate of interest and limited in tolls to the amount necessary to retire and pay interest on the bonds. Experience with private bridges is that they result in large profits to stockholders and other private parties and the maintenance of high tolls.
He also said:
Private bridges of this kind bring with them approach and traffic problems which in the end fall on the state and the municipalities, and what looks at first like a purely private business proposition becomes a public problem of traffic and planning affecting all the surround ing territory. Obviously, these related prob lems which go with such a structure can onlj be properly solved by a public authority.
I have just signed a measure setting up a public non-profit-making bi-state authority, similar to the port authorities of New York and Albany, to build the Champlain bridge, and also a measure providing for a study of a Niagara port and frontier authority, which, if it is established, will have the power to plan just such bridges as this without private profit and solely in the public interest. I think this project and similar bridges, such as the Grand Island bridges, can wait until a public authority is established for the purpose. I see no more reason for a franchise to a private corporation to build a bridge over the St. Lawrence than I do for a franchise or a license to a private corporation to develop the state's water-power on that stream.
That, Mr. Chairman, is the policy of the state of New York. What I anticipated has happened: the counterpart of this bill has been thrown out by the legislature of that state. In view of this, why on earth should we pass a measure giving authority to build a bridge half way? This bridge has been up in the air for some time. It started by trying to get on top of one of the other bridges; and under this bill the promoters are asking for authority to place their structure within 250 feet of the other bridge. Is that something that this parliament should authorize? I submit, Mr. Chairman, that you had better think it over again.
Where do you want the bridge?
My hon. friend need not say veiy much. His bridge on the St. Lawrence will probably fail the same as this one.

speechtext: When this bill was last before the committee we were considering clause 4.

Mr. Chairman, when this clause was before us a few days ago I made some comments on the fact that it provided for shares of no par value. I know that is becoming a rather common practice by many large corporations, but it seems to me it is not proper in the case of a public -company of this description. I think that a corporation which proposes to build a bridge for public use at an expenditure of a large sum of money should have a substantial capital. If this section were agreed to the shares would be of nominal or no par value, and the promoters could sell them at any price they pleased. I think we ought to adopt the old practice of having a specific amount of capital provided for this enterprise, divided into shares of $100 each. Therefore in accordance with the notice I gave of an amendment for this purpose which appears in votes and proceedings of March 21, I beg to move:
That the whole of section 4 be struck out and replaced by the following:
4. The capital stock of the company shall be two million dollars, divided into shares of one hundred dollars each, and may be called up by the directors from time to time as they deem necessary.
I think this amendment will be to the advantage of the company, because I suppose they intend issuing a large amount of bonds as provided for in this bill. If so, they must have some substantial capital behind them.
Amendment agreed to.

On section 20-When property, etc., to be conveyed to the Dominion.

I should like to have an

as the legislature of said state may designate, and so far as the same is situated within the Dominion of Canada shall be conveyed, without cost or expense, to the Dominion of Canada-
Does that mean any addition to the capital stock in the way of money, or does it mean the actual cost of the stock transfer? What does it mean?

As I pointed out before when a similar bill was before the house this clause is a perfect farce. Not only is it farcical but it is deceptive. It says that at some time the mortgage bonds outstanding may be redeemed by means of receipts from tolls, and the stock may be retired by means of these receipts, and then, when this is accomplished the American part of the bridge shall be conveyed to the state of Michigan and the Canadian part to the Dominion of Canada. Now what are the conditions? First this company, under this clause, may pay up its entire capital of $2,500,000 under a provision whereby it can transfer any asset of any value to the company and issrue therefore its stock as fully paid up. Therefore the $2,500,000 of capital stock in this company may, under the advice of any competent legal counsel, be issued for practically no actual value at all -a thousand dollars or one hundred dollars, or some nominal value, will pay up the stock. Then there is another provision in the bill that the stock must be paid off at the price fixed by the by-laws of the company. That is, assuming that each share of $100 par value was actually paid up in cash, the directors, by their resolution and of their own will, may provide that the stock which costs $100 in cash, even if paid up in cash, shall be redeemed at $100, $200, $300, $400 or any price they see fit. So that the proposal now held out that this public utility undertaking, after it has earned sufficient to redeem these mortgage bonds, and after it has earned sufficient to retire its capital stock, shall be handed over and become the property of the Dominion of Canada, is entirely farcical and deceptive, because it leads to the impression that, after the actual cash invested in the bridge is paid off out of the tolls of the company, it would then become the property of the Dominion government. Then to further mislead, it seems to me, those who drafted this bill have added at the end of section 20:
Provided always that the period for payment of the obligations of the companies and the retirement of their capital stock and any extension thereof and the provision of the companies' by-laws in respect thereof shall have been previously approved by the governor in council.

But bylaws dealing with the prices to be paid are not, under that act, subject to the approval of the governor in council. I called attention to that fact before. I cannot propose an amendment now; but it seems to me that this whole clause should be struck out; that we should not be parties to a farcical and deceptive section such as is inserted in this bill, which offers no opportunity to the government to exercise a proper discretion, and which really holds out the suggestion that this bridge will one day become the public property of the Dominion of Canada, while it rests entirely with the directors of the company to designate and fix the price at which it shall become the property of the Dominion.

that would afford some relief. As the matter stands now, the whole thing is in the hands of the company. They could pass an extreme by-law which would never be approved and the country would never get the bridge.

There are two reasons, in my humble judgment, why this proposed resolution as now redrafted is beyond the scope of the notice given in the votes and proceedings.
First, by stating that provision should be made for the administration of "school lands" in addition to school lands endowment funds, the mover has materially changed the conditions on which the proposed grant of their natural resources should, in his opinion, be made to the interested provinces.
Secondly, the words "but in compliance with the letter and spirit of the constitution," were placed in the first draft so as to apply

to the granting of the natural resources to the prairie provinces; whilst in the second draft these words have been moved further down and made to apply to the administration of school land endowment funds for educational purposes. There is a material difference between the two propositions.
The difference is such that the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan)- who is a lawyer of outstanding ability known not only in Montreal but throughout Canada, and I may say North America-said that, if the original motion which appeared in the votes and proceedings was moved to-day he would vote against it but that in its latter form he would support it. I am only making this reference to show that evidently there has been a material change in the resolution. However, if the house were willing to give unanimous consent to the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington, personally I would be pleased to listen to the debate. But strictly speaking, and according to the rules of the house, this motion is out of order.
I will quote in support of my ruling, May, 13th edition, page 234; Blackmore, page 212; Redlich, second volume, pages 216 and 217, and a footnote; and Bourinot, 4th edition, page 299. Bourinot is very clear on the matter. He says:
A motion on the order paper must be in accordance with the notice in the votes; and, should a member desire to substitute another, or alter its terms, he must first obtain the leave of the house.
Under the circumstances I cannot do otherwise than rule that the point of order is well taken.
May I say this to hon. members:	All the
authorities state that when an alteration is proposed to be made to a motion the mover should inform the Speaker himself. In the present case I was informed only by what I read on the order paper. It is true that as regards technical changes a member may address himself to the Clerk or one of the officials who draft motions for members, but when a material change is made I should be informed of it. By failure to do this the hon. member loses his turn whilst if he had notified me the other day I would have told him at once that such alterations involved the loss by him of his place on the order paper.

If you will kindly permit me, Mr. Speaker, I should be very sorry if you thought for a moment that there was any intention on my part to manifest any disrespect towards you.

International Peace*-Miss Macphail
I do not say that disrespect enters at all into the question.
I really did not consider the change to be material. However, I conform to your ruling at once, and I will ask the Clerk to strike the motion off the order paper.
Does the hon. gentleman wTant to drop the motion?
Is there anything else to do?

Is it the pleasure of the
house that the hon. gentleman have leave to withdraw his motion?
Motion withdrawn.

Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey) moved:
That, in the opinion of this house, the time has come for the establishment of a government department for the promotion of peace and international understanding.
She said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to this motion asking for the establishment of a department to work for peace and international understanding, I assume that all hon. members in this chamber are anxious to bring security to our country, and that any differences we have in the matter relate to the methods to be employed in bringing about peace rather than to any doubt as to the desirability of securing peace. I conclude that we all want to have security at home and friendship abroad. At one time almost everyone, possibly indeed everyone, had confidence in military preparedness and war as methods of bringing about security and of settling international differences. But I think that no one will now deny that that confidence in military preparedness and in war which used to be so complete has been very much shaken. Still while some to-day have simply scrapped the old way and have found a new method, and are relying upon the development of good will as the greatest security that we could find, there are others who, while they have not perfect confidence in war or in preparedness for war, still think of these methods as the best to adopt. Then there are others of our citizens and of citizens of the world who stand between the two ideas and are not quite sure in which faith to rely. The last war with its frightful loss of life and treasure caused all of us to think of this subject as one of very great importance. Not 56103-108i
only did Canada lose sixty thousand of her very best men, but the world lost ten million of its best men, and if we are going to view this question from the point of view of humanity we must consider that loss of ten million young men a dead loss and one that will cause concern to every citizen in the world, including the citizens of Canada.
The cost of the last war was greater than that of any previous war, although all wars and all preparations for wars in the past have been exceedingly costly. So great has been the cost of preparing for and carrying out wars that in the first twenty years of the twentieth century, fourteen countries spent the fantastic sum of $61,000,000,000 in preparation for and carrying out war. England alone to-day spends on war or preparation for war fourteen shillings out of every twenty shillings of her national expenditure. The United States spend 82 cents out of every dollar on war or preparation for war. The total debt of the United States prior to th* war was $1,125,000,000 and to-day it stands at between $18,000,000,000 and $19,000,000,000. How much greater even that that-and that is a terrific increase-must be the increase in the debt of such countries as France and Germany because of the war? In Canada the exact figures are not available, but certainly more than fifty cents out of every dollar of our national expenditure go to pay for wars past and preparation for wars to come. Some claim-and they may have figures to substantiate their claim, but I do not have them under my hand-that two-thirds of every dollar of Canada's expenditure goes for this purpose. When one thinks of these figures, the amount of money involved alone, one thinks of what the spending of this money for the good of the people could have done. I have not any doubt at all that had the one fantastic sum I mentioned of $61,000,000,000 been spent to bring knowledge, a high standard of living and happiness to the common peoples of the world, wars would by now not be necessary. The house, however, may not agree with me in that. More and more people are coming to believe, and even people in high places are stating quite fearlessly, that they believe security must come by means other than military preparedness. There are many statesmen one could quote, but I am going to confine myself to very brief quotations. The first one is Field Marshal Sir William Robertson, who was Chief of the Imperial General Staff from 1915 to 1918. That is, he was a military man trained in military tactics, and indeed he must have been a very successful one to have filled that position in those stressful yearn
1694	COMMONS
International Peace-Miss Macphail
In speaking of war-I am quoting from The U.F.A. of December 15, 1927, and this report appeared also in the daily press of a few days previous-he said:
War has become a wholly detestable thing, and is almost, if not quite, as disastrous to victors as to vanquished.
Never in history were preparations so complete or so widespread as during the fifty or sixty years previous to 1914, and yet never were wars so frequent as in that period.
A little later on in the same speech he is reported to have said:
Every man and woman should energetically support all efforts made for devising some more sensible and humane way of composing international differences than the destructive and futile methods upon which reliance has hitherto been unsuccessfully placed.
That is the only conclusion I can reach after a military career covering on Sunday next, a period of exactly fifty years.
So that this great British gentleman, who had been trained in a military school for fifty years, comes to the conclusion, speaking first, I suppose, for British men and women, and afterwards for all men and women, that they should set themselves to the task of finding some other and better way of settling international disputes.
Every one was sorry and grieved at the death quite recently of Field Marshal Haig. I wonder if we are willing to honour his memory by heeding his words. On one occasion he said:
I urge you to a crusade having for its object the freeing of the whole world from the devastating scourge of war.
I might mention too such outstanding work for a new international spirit as was done in Great Britain by E. D. Morrell, now gone, and as has been done by Lord Robert Cecil, Ramsay MacDonald and the Right Hon. Arthur Ponsonby. These are all men of high standing in British public life and they all take the stand that we shall not get security through military preparedness; that we are simply wasting money, and that military preparedness cannot bring about the thing we are seeking for, namely, security at home and goodwill and friendship abroad.
Whatever may be the opinion of members of this house as to the degree of military preparedness necessary, or as to the advisability of disarmament, I think every hon. member will agree that such things as ignorance, suspicion and fear must be got rid of before we can have permanent peace. While it is true that other things cause war, these three, ignorance, suspicion and fear, leave the common people of all countries the prey to the propagandist in the hours of crisis. It makes them willing to bear these crushing burdens of
UVliss Macphail.]
debt caused by armaments, because, through lack of knowledge, they are led to believe that they must endure this staggering taxation in order to bring security to themselves in their own country. We have not in Canada, and indeed not to any extent anywhere in the world, studied constructively the art of making peace or the technique of peace. I think the technique of war has been studied by some of the most astute minds in all countries; but had the same amount of energy, had the same wealth, had the same knowledge of the psychology of the people been used to promote peace as has been and is yet being used in Canada to promote preparedness for war-because I am afraid it is still being done -we would to-day be far on our way towards the settlement of international disputes by some method other than war, and it would be true to-day that the institution of war in Canada would not be the respected institution it is.	No one can doubt that in
Canada the institution of war is a most respected one which the " best people " like very much. I have noticed that these people, when questioned, do not admit it; but in following the votes of money and the comments in the house on the subject of war, one cannot help concluding that the institution of war is still a respected one. I view this condition with alarm.
I do not however question the patriotism of those people in the house and in the country who believe that that is the way to be a patriotic citizen. I grant quite freely that they are patriotic people and they are working for what they believe is the best thing for their country. I simply question their wisdom, not their patriotism. On the other hand, often in the past in this house, the patriotism of people like myself and those who think with me has been questioned. They think we are not patriotic, that we do n.ot love our country. One might ask, what is patriotism? Surely it is loyalty to a group; but sometimes we forget that we owe loyalty to many groups. We cannot have too much loyalty, either absolutely or in comparison with the loyalty of other peoples. But we can have too much loyalty to one group, forgetting the other groups to which we also belong. We are more and more coming to know that everyone of us belongs to that group which is known as humanity, and that we do owe a very great loyalty to that largest group of all-humanity. For Canadians, for a Britisher, for a citizen who is a member of the British commonwealth of nations, it should not be difficult to build a larger loyalty out of our present loyalties, because

International Peace-Miss Macphail
our loyalties have grown to include not only our own country and the mother country, but a group of countries winch cover a large part of the surface of the earth. Surely then we ought to be willing, and mentally and spiritually able, to take the lead in the world in developing a still larger loyalty that will not stop until it has included the whole shrinking world. It is worthy of note, too, that patriotism is not an innate thing; it is cultivated, and it will be just what we train it to be. If we train the children and the young people of this country to view patriotism as a very much bigger thing than we have thought of it in the past, then within one generation, if we set about it with decision and a desire to win, we shall have a new patriotism, which, while not making light of the love of our own country, will expand to cover the needs of all countries.
Canada's position geographically makes her a country that is important in the history of the world at this moment. Geographically we belong to one continent. Politically we belong to another continent. There is no good reason why we cannot be the interpreter of the one continent to the other. Then, too, the Canadian mind is used to a large framework. Canada is a large, if not too thickly populated, country, and the Canadian mind can move with ease from Halifax to Vancouver, surely with much more ease than the European mind can move over the same distance. That should make it easy for us to give the world a lead in learning to cover mentally a larger space. The international mind is really nothing more than a mind that does not stop at the borders of one's own country, but bridges that gap that lies between one's own country and other countries, and bridges it sympathetically.
Canada is young. As countries go, we are merely a youth, and youth always looks to the future. In looking to the future, and not to the present, we must all realize that we need to build the security of the world on something more stable than military preparedness. We have had since the end of the great war a very great many memorials to the brave who gave their lives in the service of their country during that awful conflict. My own personal opinion is that many of the memorials which are supposed to lead us to think of the service and love and devotion of those who died simply glorify the institution of war. I think that the formation of a peace department would be a fitting commemoration of tLe devotion and sacrifice of the 60,000 Canadians who died, if we remember what was said during the war and directly after, fignting a war that
was to end war. We have at the front of this building a tower which is called a peace tower. I was greatly interested in going through it and looking over it carefully, and my conclusion was that it is a very equisite piece of work, but that it is misnamed. No one who looks over it carefully can call it a peace chamber. It so clearly, one might almost say so brazenly, though beautifully, glorifies the institution of war. That sort of thing will never lead the young men and young women of Canada to think of new methods. It will simply lead them to think of the glory of the old; and it is not a fair way of putting the thing up to the young people of Canada, because the truth of war is not told, only the glory of war, not the misery, not the death, not the disease, not the broken hearts, not the shattered lives. Nothing of that is told at all; it is just the glory of war. I wonder who named the tower the peace tower. It is a queer idea of peace. A name will not bring us peace, I am sure of that.
Canada since the world war has been drawn more and more into world currents. There is an evidence of that in our appointing ambassadors to the different countries of the world. We have also been given a place on the council of the league of nations. All these things show that we are, whether we like it or not, becoming citizens of the world. But up until now very little of anything has been done by the Canadian people or the Canadian government to prepare Canadians for the new responsibilities which are ours. A department of peace would act as a focus or centre for peace thinking and peace activities. While there are some engaged in peace thinking and peace activities at the present time in Canada, they are scattered, and they have no help from-well, I will leave it at that: they have no help. They are the rank and file of the people, many of them, and it is hard for them to get the knowledge they desire. There has been no lead given in peace activities in Canada, with one or two notable exceptions which I shall mention later.
I believe that under the British North America Act the Dominion government has jurisdiction over war and peace in so far as control rests in Canada. It is therefore the business of the Dominion government, rather than of the provincial governments to help the people to find some new way of settling international disputes. Canada has a long and indeed a very honourable history in the settling of disputes through conciliation, and the most noted of all is the Rush-Bagot treaty which was made at the end of the war of 1812-
1696	COMMONS
International Peace-Miss Macphail
14. Ia the histories which I studied and from which I taught this treaty was given some prominence. To be exact, I think some sixteen pages were devoted to the history of the war and two paragraphs to the peace, but still two paragraphs was something. They told, and told sympathetically, of the importance of the Rush-Bagot treaty, which disarmed the border line between Canada and the United States, which from that time on has been an example in peaceful settlement to the whole world. But in the new histories now used in Ontario, a copy of which I now hold in my hand, as many pages are devoted to the war, but there is not one single line devoted to the Rush-Bagot treaty; it is not even mentioned. I am not familiar with the history texts used in the other provinces, but the children in the schools of Ontario reading these histories do not know anything about the Rush-Bagot treaty, do not know anything about the greatest incident of that period of the history of United States and Canada, because no one will doubt that the peace treaty was much more important than the war. This treaty shows that Canada in the past has been interested in finding new methods rather than relying on the old. In the case of the Rush-Bagot treaty we prepared for peace, and we had peace. I think that is logical. The old idea that if you prepare for war you will have peace is a fallacy. If you prepare for war you will have war, and if you prepare for peace you will have peace.
The International Joint Commission, which has been in existence for some seventeen years and has settled over twenty differences between Canada and the United States, has been mentioned twice, just lately, in far-flung parts of the world. I am quoting from an editorial that appeared in the Citizen of March 1, 1928:
Recently Charles Evans Hughes spoke of conciliation between Canada and the United States at the Pan-American Conference in Havana, where he submitted the plan of the International Joint Commission as a model method of maintaining peaceful relations between neighbouring countries. A few days later, the League of Nations security committee at Geneva listened with keen interest to a description of the working of the commission. The Canadian member of the committee Dr. W. A. Riddell, told how this model scheme of conciliation has worked successfully in dealing with over twenty cases in the last seventeen years. He recommended the adoption of simlar permanent boards of conciliation between other nations whose frontiers adjoin.
The editorial continues:
Dr. Riddell urged that security could be increased more by disarmament than by miltary measures.

I want the government to tell us if Dr. Riddell was speaking on their behalf. If so, are not the words which he used in Geneva and the action of the government in straight contradiction? If it is true that security comes through disarmament, then why is it that our military estimates have been increased from eleven million dollars in 1925 to eighteen million dollars this year? An explanation is due the country. The hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) recently addressed the Ottawa branch of the League of Nations Association and gave expression of his views. He said:
The only way of securing peace is by what is usually called moral disarmament, and that moral disarmament can be obtained only when a strong public opinon, the opinion in the shops, in the factories, on the farms, in the universities, in the schools, when opinion everywhere is deeply and intimately convinced that war is a calamity and the worst of all calamities.
These are noble words, and I feel that the hon. minister believes in their truth. So I am going to suggest to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) that for the good of Canada and the good of the world 'he request the Minister of Justice and the Minister of National Defence to exchange portfolios. I anticipate the Prime Minister will say that he does not want to form a new department. Personally I am quite willing to accept a department of defence through security and goodwill, with the bon. Minister of Justice at its head, if he is allowed to do what he wants to do. In looking over the personnel of the cabinet I have often been puzzled to discover who are the military members. Who are they? They all look so peaceable that I am amazed at what is happening. It is quite clear that some of the ministers are pushing things from the military side. There is no excuse-if there is, I shall be glad to hear it-for the increase in our military estimates, and for the aggressive development of war psychology in the Dominion.
I do not wish dogmatically to lay down what a department of peace might do, but I hope I shall not tire the house too much by offering a few suggestions as to the work of such a department. I would have suggested by resolution a peace bureau either in the Department of External Affairs or the Department of Secretary of State, but I did not wish it to be shoved off into a corner while a department to bring security through military measures was given a better place. Already we have a full-fledged department of war, although I notice that in the debate on the motion of the hon. member for Wetaski-

International Peace-Miss Macphail
win (Mr. Irvine) the Minister of National Defence said that his department is not preparing for war, but for peace; that really he is a minister of peace. I am glad to hear it, but in the face of the activities of his department I regret to say there is nothing on which I can rest my belief, much as I should like to accept his declaration.
A department of peace should be twofold in character. First, it should have general supervision of an extensive program for peace throughout Canada. Secondly, it should cultivate friendly relations with other countries by promoting our knowledge of other people with regard to their cultural, moral and social achievements. This would be very interesting to Canadians, and we have very much to learn along this line. Then, too, it should encourage the work of international institutions, including the League of Nations, and make known their work to our people, so that we would be made acquainted with all the machinery that has been set up in any part [DOT]f the world for finding new methods of settling international difficulties. I think that such a department should also study the causes of war, and by frank discussion present evidence revealing the wastefulness and ineffectiveness of war. It might also make clear to our people some of our own mannerisms that offend the sensibilities of other nations. I do think we have a British superiority complex which must be very offensive to other nations, and cannot be making any contribution to the harmony'of the world. This department would quite naturally work in cooperation with all agencies that wanted the data and other material which it would collect. It would develop the will to peace through education by working with peace societies, schools, churches, labour associations, women's, farmers' and social clubs, and any other Canadian agencies whose efforts in the direction of peace could be made more effective by such co-operation. The department could also prepare a list of speakers, who, while not employed by the government, could, through the department, be made available for addressing public meetings-speakers who were authorities on some one phase of this great question. Our government departments issue booklets, pamphlets, posters and films, and there seems to be no good reason why a department of peace could not use the same means to make known to the Canadian people the truths regarding peace and war.
And how little money it would cost the government to make a gift of books for the promotion of peace. These books could be issued to our public and school libraries. We have Rhodes scholarships in this country.
We might establish peace scholarships on a somewhat similar plan, allotting a scholarship to each province. The Rhodes scholarships I think are confined to young men, but I would want these peace scholarships available to young women as well. The winners of these scholarships would go abroad each year to study along lines which would make them better world citizens and at the same time better citizens of Canada.
It has occurred to me-I do not claim any originality for the idea-that we might very well establish a yearly peace award for the best work done in the cause of peace. This award I suggest should be given by the government and might be confined to Canadians or be made open to the citizens of any country. The award would not be confined necessarily to the greatest contribution scholastically to the peace of the world, but to the best work to this end along any line.
We have a military college where young men are prepared to be warriors. Why not establish a college to train young men in promoting peaceful understandings throughout the world? This would be far better work and those engaged in it would become mucn better citizens, with all respect to the graduates from the military college. Then instead of making grants for the training of cadets in summer camps-and but for these grants the cadet movement would not continue for another five years-the government might use the money to much better purpose for the establishment of summer schools to promote the study of international friendship. I imagine a great many Canadians would be glad to get together for a few weeks to secure a better understanding than they possess today of the problems of the world. In fact I should think that the work of this department would be very interesting; it would be unlimited, adventurous and wholly positive rather than destructive as is military training at the present time. Such a department would call to the highest in us; it would call out our mental and spiritual attributes, challenging them, rather than the physical, which is on the lowest possible plane.
My words this afternoon may seem quite futile; all words on this subject may seem futile. But what are disarmament conferences, even conferences of the League of Nations, conferences to promote good will, unless they are backed by a conviction on the part of the peoples of the world, the common people, the rank and file of the nations? It is my opinion- it may or may not be right-that the common people of Canada, certainly the farmers, and I believe the common people generally, are exceedingly concerned that the government,
1698	COMMONS
International Peace-Miss Macphail
and we working together with the government, shall strive to find1 some new way of settling international disputes. The common people are sick of war; they are tired of the glorification of it. The swank that goes with it to-day does not carry much force in the country. In international politics, as in everything else, the misfortune is that our aim is too low. The real crime after all is low aim, and by aiming high the government or any international body will call out the latent idealism of the common people. And after all the latent idealism of the common people is the greatest force for peace in the world to-day.
In closing I would ask the government not to consider the matter lightly, because it is not a trivial subject; it includes within itself all others and is the most important subject facing mankind' to-day. If we do not find some new way there is nothing surer than that, if we keep on for another twenty-five years as we' have been going since 1918, we shall have another war whether we like it or not. Nothing can prevent it if we keep preparing for war.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
I have very
much pleasure in supporting the motion. Sometimes when we try to appraise the fruits of the great war our hearts ache at the seeming dearth of results, but I think we shall all agree that one fruit of the war of a moral nature was of extreme value to us, and that was the reaction in the minds of people everywhere against the very idea of war. That, to me, is the most solid result of the war, but apart from that I cannot see anything except results which are almost too pathetic to mention. That, however, was a solid gain-the reaction of civilization against the very conception of war. But that reaction was of a diffuse character, existing in the minds of people as a fleeting sentiment, tending as the years have gone by to evaporate. With succeeding years, as I apprehend, it will tend to disperse more speedily until the only substantial fruit of war will have vanished. I think it is the duty of every civilized people somehow before it is too late to crystallize that widespread sentiment against war into something that will make it effective. This is the duty we owe to our brave men who to-day sleep beneath a foreign sod. There is nothing on earth we can do for them but that-to bring this idea to a focus.
_ We all agree that the spectral evil of war is largely psychological in character. As Emerson once said, it is a thought that has created these armaments and it is a thought that will disperse them. But how is this 
thought to emerge which is going to displace the devilish thought that created war? There is no other way of creating that thought except by the organized effort of a nation's intelligence, and it is our duty, especially as legislators, to see that .that superseding thought shall make itself felit. It cannot be done by spasmodic effort; it cannot be done by the efforts of individuals; it cannot be done by the churches alone. They are all doing their best. The only effective effort can be made by a nation in its organized capacity, by parliament.
There are very many practical ways in which a government bureau of some kind could bring the nation's sentiment with respect to war to bear effectively upon world peace. In the first place such a bureau might very well undertake to purge the sources of our information in regard to international matters. The press of the world has many very outstanding qualities which we all admire, but as a medium of international information it has ceased to claim the trust of intelligent people. The necessities of war are responsible very largely for this psychology on the part of the people and the feeling that they can no longer trust the ordinary channels of international information. One thing we all regret is the fact that the various agencies by which international information was conveyed to us during the war received an almost fatal moral twist. The supposed necessities of war impelled the authorities to use the press not to enlighten but to drug the people. I remember two or three years ago going through the archives of Canada and seeing under a glass cover a medal representing the sinking of the Lusitania. I was given to understand that this medal had been actually struck by the German people during the war to commemorate that atrocity. Some time afterwards, however, travelling on the train, I fell into conversation with a gentleman who at one time had occupied a prominent position in the government of Canada and he informed me that the medal had been struck for propaganda purposes. Whether or not that is true we know that during the war the intelligence of the people was drugged by very similar methods, so the privately owned press no longer has the confidence of intelligent people with respect to international matters. It seems to me that a government organization could fulfil a very useful purpose in cleansing the channels of information with respect to international affairs. As we all know, an increasing interest is being taken in the possibilities of the radio, and I am sure the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself is not slow in sensing the great

International Peace-Mr. Bird
possibilities of that method of dispensing information. Here, right to our hands, is a means almost providential whereby the government, through a proper organization, could keep the people from one end of Canada to the other accurately informed upon current international affairs. Thus there would be gradually created a thought which would ultimately displace the diabolic thought which will otherwise very soon lead to another world catastrophe.
Another means of activity which might vety well be made use of is education. While that is not especially a function of this government, through various means of co-operation I think such a bureau could be made useful in working with the provincial educational authorities to expurgate our school books of those elements which build up in our children a phy-chology with regard to war which in all ages has proved to be as tinder waiting for the opportune spark. One of the things wdiich has been and is being wrongly taught in our schools is the subject of history, and I think we can all remember to our regret the twist which our minds received during the elementary period of our education with regard to important facts in history. Personally, I was always taught that France was the traditional enemy of England, and that every school child in England had that fact drilled into his consciousness. I was also taught that Germany was the traditional friend of England, and that teaching remained in the British school books until 1914. With respect to almost everything of an international character, our children have received the wrong slant; history has been taught inaccurately, perhaps not with respect to the facts but certainly with respect to the emphasis. Wrong emphases have been placed, and the expected result has been achieved. I was reading the other day about that famous incident in history when King Charles I lost his head in 1649. That fact has entered into our school books and our system of education to an extent of which it was not worthy. On the other hand, just four years earlier an Englishman introduced into English agriculture that very humble vegetable the swede turnip, but do you think English school children ever heard anything about the introduction of the swede turnip? They heard about the head of Charles I but the turnip was worth a great deal more than the head of that king, because the head of King Charles I brought nothing but trouble to English politics, while we are told that the swede turnip in succeeding years was the means of helping England win the battles of Waterloo
and Trafalgar. I just mention that to illustrate the manner in which history has been twisted for purely chauvinistic purposes, and I think a bureau of this kind could very well start to work in co-operation with our provinces to correct some of these false ideas. I wish I had time to enter into that phase of the question a little more fully because I believe it lies at the very roots of the menace of war.
Let me refer very briefly to another job Which faces parliament, and to deal with which parliament should have a proper agent.
I have already referred to this false patriotism which has grown up in Canadian hearts and which, to our sorrow, very frequently finds its characteristic expression. Viscount Cecil recently said that the prime causes of war were, first, a traditional officialism, and secondly, chauvinism, or a false and narrow patriotism. Chauvinism is not confined to any one class; it is something of which we are all guilty in a greater or less degree and it is something of which our hearts and minds must be purged before the world can be made safe against the menace of war. I sometimes think of the way in which we make use of our national anthem, that hymn which means so much to the British people;
I think sometimes we carry things a little too far through our habit of using that hymn upon many occasions and for many purposes in connection with which its use was never intended. I am also afraid that our national flag is many times used in a manner unworthy of its glorious symbolism. That flag should not be the symbol of anything narrow, anything national in the chauvinistic sense. What is the flag of which we are so proud? That flag represents a Roman gibbet thrice superimposed upon a square of coloured bunting. WTe all know what took place on that Roman gibbet; we all know of the scene that was enacted there, and we have no right to make that the symbol of a narrow nationalism, because it was the symbol of a universalism, the spirit which is against war and for human co-operation. I see no hope for the future of civilization if we allow our patriotism to become narrow. We have a great many Canadian poets still living, and there is a great opportunity for some of them to write something for Canada, perhaps not to supersede the hymns we already have, but to represent the spirit of Canada as that spirit has been maintained since the great war; something to represent the broad outlook of the average Canadian with regard to world affairs. As it is, I should rather have a single line of one of the lyrics of Lampman, Campbell, Scott, or any of our

International Peace-Mr. Evans
Canadian poets, than a lot of the doggerel that passes as patriotic song. After all, I want my children to get something of the spirit that some of our own poets have put into their simple lines that speak of the Canadian spirit as it has grown up amongst the beautiful objects of Canadian scenery. There is a great scope in Canada for building up the type of patriotism that will be an example to the wide world. We have all the conditions, both material and moral, which will make for a new type of feeling with respect to our country.
Such a bureau, if I may so term it, would have the effect of declaring what Canada's moral attitude is on the question of peace. Simply because here and there you have sentiments eloquently expressed does not mean to say that we as a people have taken a moral stand on the question. We heard a lot before the war about the will to power, an attitude that had got beyond mere sentiment and ideas and had embodied itself into a national attitude. It is fully time that we Canadians should cease to talk sentimentally about peace, or even go further to expound our ideals about peace, and that we should assume once and for all a moral attitude on the question-that we should have the will to peace. And how can we do it unless we organize the wealth of intelligence we have at our command?

After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to support this resolution because I believe the time has come for Canada and the empire to find means of preserving peace by outlawing war in place of the old method of being prepared for war as a means of national safety. The time is now ripe for the outlawry of war and violence, and this nation cannot spend a few thousand dollars any better than in fostering the idea of peace by educational methods and propaganda that will in the end reach the hearts and minds of the common people to the extent that governments will have to change their minds in regard to preparation as a means of national security. War again, if carried on by any nation which has no scruples about winning by any means whatsoever, will be more likely to win in the future by the slaughter of the innocents than by contests between trained armies. This fact alone should, I think, make it imperative to educate 
the electors of all countries rather than attempt to bring about the outlawry of war by governments who are more than likely to represent the big interests, the money lenders and others interested in big business.
The fact is that war has been robbed of its glory by mechanization. The glamour of battle no longer exists. War is nothing more now than butchery on a wholesale scale, and the common people, women and children as well as men, are the sufferers. For this reason it ought to be considered the logical thing to do to outlaw the whole business of war. The flame of war is fed by national budgets and it is time that Canada worked to douche that flame and lead in the cause of peace through education. Our estimates to-day are illogical in face of the position that we have taken on the League of Nations, and I hope that we shall consider this. The position is so illogical as to be untenable. What we want to do now is to remove as far as possible all machinery that makes for war and create instead an institution to foster peace. I believe Canada is in just such a position that any move on her part in this direction will have an effect on other nations, and, being a part of the British Empire, we may well by this means set an example that will be a precedent to other nations and will help to move forward the cause of international cooperation.
According to the Free Press of Winnipeg of September 7 last, an associated press cable from Geneva states that a concerted attempt to revise the Geneva protocol stands forth as a possibility in the League of Nations. Van Brooklands of the Netherlands actually introduced a resolution calling for a revival of the principles of that protocol, with the serious discussion thereof, to the end that an attempt be made to outlaw war. Canada has nothing to fear in moving in this way. Our civilization has reached a point of advance by which we may measure the degree of its peril when its survival depends on the willingness of the great masses of the citizens of all nations to stand loyally together as comrades in this great venture. I look upon the League of Nations to-day as the symbol of that great outstanding fact. Co-operation has become a world-wide necessity of the present age. The downfall of civilization is the alternative to co-operation, according to the opinion to-day of many great men writing in the greatest journals and magazines. H. G. Wells says that it is a race between cooperation and ruin. The progress of civilization does not consist, as some would have us believe, in a gradual advance to a point

International Peace-Mr. Ralston
of safety. It consists rather in a growing perception of the common risk, and a growing willingness on the part of the common people in all countries to face this together. Cooperative effort of the nations is needed and it calls for leadership and valour to initiate and take part in a movement such as this resolution calls for. I am glad to see that the common sense of the people of Great Britain and the United States has prevailed on both governments to cut down on their war expenditures for this year.
Civilization has advanced scientifically, we must admit, and it has advanced behind the shelter of big guns, but we are face to face now with the time when big guns will not avail to protect civilization. We have to face the fact that the advance of our civilization will be along lines of co-operation, or, to give it a clearer definition, a sympathetic feeling for the rights of all others through co-operation. The advance of civilization and the safety of mankind lie in the unity of that great resolve to co-operate, and it is time now that we in Canada went forward in the cause of peace and education. No other nation on earth to-day is so advantageously situated to establish a system of education that will wean the viewpoint of the common people away from preparedness through great armaments and great guns to a system of education and co-operation.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to occupy
the attention of the house for only a very few minutes, and it is because the mover of the resolution (Miss Macphail) in her address has felt it necessary to discuss along with this resolution the matter of national defence. I thank the hon. member very sincerely for the suggestion she has made as to the exchange of portfolios, but apparently I am not, according to the evening newspapers, likely to achieve such an exchange; so in view of the fact that I am still in the position to which I have been called by His Excellency, I want to say just a word or two with regard to the general subject matter, and more particularly as it concerns my department.
The hon. member opened by stating that there were three different classes in the world, and three different opinions held, with regard to the matter of national security. One was the class which regarded armament as being the only method of achieving national security; another was the class which looked altogether towards peace and disarmament as the only method of attaining that end, and the third class was made up of those who were irresolute between those two opinions.
She did, I think, leave out what I consider to be a very important class, the one to which I myself belong, and that is the class which believes in both those methods as a means of achieving national security, namely, that we must seek to maintain our national position by taking all reasonable means to preserve our security against attack by force, and at the same time work along the lines which she and others have suggested to bring about the situation where defence forces will not be needed. I believe that two-fold view is the position taken my many countries of the world to-day. I believe that it is the position of Canada. I believe that is the position of many men and women who, from the bottom of their hearts-just as deeply as my hon. friend does-feel that war is anything but a glorious thing, that war is the last resort, that war is one thing we want to get rid of just as quickly as possible. But while they are striving in every way possible to get rid of war, they realize that we live in a practical world, a world where we must take reasonable steps to maintain national security even while we seek to attain our ideals of international peace. The effect of our ministers preaching the gospel in the city of Ottawa Sunday after Sunday is not I think effaced by the fact that we have to maintain a police force which protects those ministers, and once in a while might have to protect the church as well. That is the attitude I take with regard to these matters, and it has been and will be my endeavour, so long as I occupy the portfolio of defence, to stress the second phase of the work of preserving national security just as much as the first, and to contribute in any way I possibly can to a removal of the causes of war. But when we remember that as far back as the sixteenth century there was a scheme for the confederation of Europe which was to do away with war; when we remember the holy alliance entered into in the early part of the nineteenth century, the conferences of Berlin and Vienna, and the Hague conferences-a great forward step in the peace of nations-and that war nevertheless came, it seems to me we still have to maintain national security by way of defence forces to a moderate degree. Perhaps the most concentrated and sustained effort ever made in the history of the world has been made in the last ten years in an endeavour to do away with this monster, war, and I do believe that the nations to-day have their attention focused on that objective more than ever before; but at the same time defence forces have to be maintained until that object is achieved.	.
1702	COMMONS
International Peace-Mr. Ralston
I want to allude just for a moment to the reference of my hon. friend who moved this resolution to the matter of an increase in the defence estimates. I know I shall have an opportunity later, when the house goes into committee to discuss this matter more fully, but I want to remind the house now that the defence estimates as laid on the table to-day, covering the militia and naval services, amount to less than one million dollars more than estimates for these same services in 1913-14 and in 1914-15. I want to remind the house also of this, that the dollar in 1913-14 purchased and provided a good deal more in the way of Clothing and equipment and supplies than the dollar does to-day. In 1913-14 there were trained at camp and at headquarters over 60,000 men, while the estimates this year provide for the training of something like 33,000 men. In 1913-14 we provided, I think, for sixteen days training in a number of the services; to-day we are providing for twelve days training. So I can assure my hon, friends that more is not being done than seems to be absolutely necessary if we are to maintain even a modest and efficient defence force.
My hon. frined the mover of the resolution deplored the fact that sufficient attention was not being paid in this country to the promotion of peace. I thoroughly agree that the education of the people of this country, of the everyday people like those of us who are here, is most desirable. Everything possible should be done to bring to the knowledge of the citizens of this country what is sought to be accomplished in connection with the league of nations; in connection with the Washington conference, which was continued in Europe last summer; in connection with the preparatory commission which is now considering the matter of disarmament; in connection with the Locarno pact; in connection with the Geneva protocol, which was mentioned by my hon. friend a few moments ago-it is eminently desirable that all these things be brought to the attention of our people.
One reference made by the mover of the resolution is of interest particularly to members of this house and to citizens of this country generally. She deplored the fact that in the peace tower which surmounts this building we have nothing but things which glorify war. I feel sure that my hon. friend has visited that tower, and I hope that all hon. members have seen it. If they have not, I feel they owe it to themselves, as well as to the memory of those who are commemorated there, to see it. I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that I do not think there can be

found in this country or elsewhere anything which has less of the glorification of war than the interior of that chamber. As one enters it, one is struck by the beauty but also by the solemnity and the sadness of the place. Facing you as you go in is the altar stone presented by the people of England, on which will rest nothing to glorify war, but a book in which will be inscribed the names of some sixty-four thousand citizens of Canada who gave their lives, and over that altar will be burning perpetually a light in their remembrance. On the wall you will see panels depicting different scenes, in the war. Very little to glorify war will be found there. One picture I remember represents Ypres, the ruins of the Cloth Hall in the foreground, with the personnel trekking their way to the front line-no glory, nothing but weariness, nothing but stress and strain. The next scene is one of trench life, and hon. members of this house know enough of that or have heard sufficiently vivid descriptions of it to make it unnecessary for me to dwell on it. Next is a village from which are coming refugees, and through which is passing a Highland battalion on its way up to duty in the front line.	Next a working party
engaged in the dismal task of digging trenches; next Sanctuary Wood, of sacred memory to Canada, with St. Eloi craters and ruined houses; next, the basilica of Albert with the leaning statue of the virgin; next the tower of Mount St. Eloi partly destroyed; next Passchendaele, with its mud and misery; next a picture of the medical corps at work with ambulances and stretcher cases, and at last a representation of ships returning to Canada leaving behind them a field of crosses watched over by a soldier resting on his arms reversed. Nothing very much suggestive of the glories of war, but something which my hon. friend might well use in any address she makes to point to the horrors of war, and to strengthen the desire and prove the necessity of getting rid of it as quickly as possible. True, one of the windows represents the call to arms; but another represents the assembly of remembrance; the third represents the thing for which my hon. friend is looking,-the dawn of peace. I say that that memorial tower has more in it perhaps than many sermons and many addresses that might be delivered at peace conferences to influence people to find as quickly as possible a method to achieve the result which not only my hon. friends who spoke a few minutes ago seek, but which we all seek. And then, as if to express the very antithesis of glorifioa-

International Peace-Mr. Manion
tion' of war, I find under a window this moving inscription from Kipling:
Nor was their agony brief, or once only imposed on them. The wounded, the war-spent, the sick received no exemption; Being cured, they returned and endured and achieved our redemption.
The sentiment of the resolution and the spirit back of it appeals, I think, to us all. The only question is how best the object can be attained. Towards that object not only our friends who have just spoken, not only this country, but practically all the countries of the world are working, and it is the duty of those of us in Canada to give the heartiest support we can in furthering that work, in doing our best to spread abroad among the nations our desire for peace, our desire that international questions may be settled by reason and not by force, and to educate our boys and girls and our citizens generally to look towards the day when arbitration, conciliation and co-operation will be accepted as the recognized means of maintaining national security.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my main reason for taking part in this debate is that unfortunately, and I know unfairly, some of our friends in the house have a tendency to suggest, if not to state expressly, that those of us who realize conditions as they exist in the world to-day, who realize that something in the shape of a national defence force is necessary, and who advocate a certain degree of national defence, are therefore advocates of war and believers in militarism. I think, sir, that suggestion is unfair, because it seems to me that it may be said, in one broad sentence, that every sane man and woman abhors war. Anyone who has seen war at close range must realize something of the horrors of that catastrophe. Long before I ever had that personal experience I did have an abhorrence of war, and even as a child I remember wondering why civilized nations that had long ago outlawed duelling -the idea that men might settle their personal disputes by guns or rapiers-could not in some way outlaw war. To-day there is a strong feeling among the civilized nations of the world that that outlawing of war should take place; but the fact remains that we cannot by ideals rule the world as a whole, that, for example, there are some tens of millions of Russians and hundreds of millions of Chinese who are not as civilized as we are, and of -whom we do not know in what direction they may happen to march if they choose to march.
In view of that fact, and of the further fact that throughout the world to-day there are
leagues and counter-leagues; that there are countries, such as Poland for instance, who fear they may be attacked by their eastern or western neighbours; that to-day Baltic and Balkan nations are quarrelling more or less among themselves, and that another such incident as the Sarajevo murder might plunge the world into a war in which we might be forced to take part-in view of all these things,
I say our sanest course is to preserve something in the shape of a nucleus for national defence. To charge that those who believe in such a course advocate war is just as ridiculous as to assert that because you believe in a police force you therefore advocate murder, arson, robbery, rape and all other crimes that a police force is maintained to prevent.
When we look at the clouds upon the European horizon, when we remember that we did not want war in 1914 but were forced into it by circumstances over which we had no control, I say it is only right that we should have something in the shape of a national defence force. I do not believe in great armaments. I am entirely of the opinion so well expressed by Sir Edward Grey in the story of his life, a life dedicated to the prevention of war in every possible way. He was the most able and most outstanding peace lover in the parliament of Great Britain, a man who for twenty-five years did everything in his power to prevent war, and yet who at last in 1914 realized that England could not keep out of the struggle that was then impending, and so joined those members of the cabinet who believed that Great Britain should uphold the sanctity of treaties and help the world against aggression by Germany. After all that experience Sir Edward Grey does take the attitude that great armaments inevitably lead to war. I entirely agree with him. But no one can charge that Canada is leading the way towards great armaments, for this country, whether under our party or the Liberal party, has simply preserved the nucleus of a defence force. That is a necessity for any self-respecting nation. I think Canada spends on her defence force the lowest amount of probably any country in the world.
