speechtext:
Some hon.
gentlemen opposite question that statement; let me give them my authority for what I say. I thought that point had come to be generally conceded, but if hon. gentlemen opposite are in any doubt I will give them the words of one or two British statesmen of whose verdict I think they will approve. I intend to quote two gentlemen, each of whom has been prime minister of Great Britain, each of whom has since passed away, but each of whom though being dead, yet speaks to us through his utterances as recorded. "What were the words of the late Andrew Bonar Law, who if I recall correctly was a member of that very administration? I quote from an English newspaper, the Newcastle Journal of November 8, 1922, in which reference is made to a speech by the late Mr. Bonar Law. These are his words in regard to the so-called Chanak incident, and with respect to the communication sent at the time to the dominions:
Towards the end of September a manifesto suddenly appeared in the newspapers. I read it with amazement. There was no consultation with the dominions, and this extraordinary manifesto was issued with the knowledge of three or four members only of the cabinet.
To suddenly throw, as a bolt from the blue, this appeal for help when not one of the dominions had the remotest idea that there was any idea of it, and when it was well known that their help could not come in time to be of any assistance in the crisis, was to risk, in my opinion one of the greatest assets of this empire. It was to take a risk with our dominions which no wise man would have taken, and which, I think, was not more foolish than it was wrong.
Then I have here the words of the late Lord Oxford and Asquith. What did he say, as reported in a Canadian Press cable to Canada
of October 8, 1922, which appeared in most of our daily papers? This report of his Bpeeeh at Dumfries on the evening of October 7th, 1922, reads as follows:
"There is every reason to believe," said Mr. Asquith, "that a week ago to-day this country, single-handed, was on the brink of an unnecessary war."
Then referring to the manifesto he said:
"All this strident rhetoric, this flag-waving and bugle-blowing, were wholly inexplicable unless the prospect of war, at any rate, was well in sight."
Mr. Asquith said he could not remember a more illtimed and discreditable incident in the whole of his public life. The effect was what might have been expected:	The French and
Italians, who were holding the neutral lines with the British, were withdrawn.
"In our great dominions," said Mr. Asquith, "were statesmen sagacious enough-let us be thankful for it-who before they committed their countries to war, required more information as to what they would be fighting for and as to how and why it had become necessary to fight at all."
May I remind the house that at the time
the manifesto was issued, Australia and New Zealand each signified their intention of sending forces to join with the British forces in the event of war. and that Canada alone stood out in seeking information and asking that her parliament be advised before the people of this country were committed to participation in another war. I quote further from the report as follows:
Referring to the question of the freedom of the straits, Mr. Asquith said the Black sea powers, particularly Russia, had just as much concern therein as Great Britain had. Moreover, the Kemalists themselves declared they were quite willing to accept the principle of the freedom of the straits. He said he saw no reason why they should not mean what they say. "What an issue that would have been to let loose the hazard of the horrors of war," Mr. Asquith exclaimed.
"Let no one be simple minded enough," said Mr. Asquith, "to suppose that the hostilities would have been confined to Chanak. Such a war would probably have involved the greater part of the Asiatic continent nearest Mesopotamia and Palestine, and possibly Egypt and other countries, with the possibility of an infinite repercussion throughout the Moslem world."
Then may I give to my hon. friends opposite the opinion of one who I think was well informed at the time, but who no one for a moment will say is an advocate of the present administration, much less of myself. I refer to Lieut.-Colonel John Bayne Maclean, of MaoLean's Magazine. What did that paper have to say with reference to this matter? Colonel Maclean, the editor, under his own name, in the issue of MacLean's
1716	COMMONS
International Peace-Mr. Mackenzie King
Magazine of November 15, 1922, published an article headed:
"Did Canada Stop Near East War? Refusal to Take Precipitous Action Saving Factor; Sane Thinking Essential to Peace."
The second paragraph of this article reads:
We were recently asked by cable to answer at once by cable that we were ready to embark on another and greater war.
Some men, not Canadians, who have unusually good sources of world-wide information, whose judgment is generally sound and whose views are held in hgh esteem, are positive that had our Premier succumbed to the Lloyd George-Churcliill demands, preceded as they were by propaganda and scheming for Canadian participation, the British Empire would undoubtedly have been at war now with Turkey, Russia and perhaps India, Afghanistan, Persia, and God knows who else or what the end would have been.
That was the opinion at that time of Colonel Maclean, and he had sources of information which I do mot hesitate to say from what I have since learned were pretty reliable. The view which he there expressed I have been told in Great Britain on very high authority was not very far from the mark as to what might have followed had Canada not taken the position which she then did.
I wish to say to my hon. friend that if this incident proves anything, it proves above all else that the spirit and the purpose and the attitude of an administration on this great question of peace and international understanding is more important than any of the lesser matters of departmental administration or departmental propaganda. The Chanak incident is only one of a number of incidents which have come up in the course of recent years, and all of which have served to disclose the essential importance of the attitude of an administration.
Take the treaty of Lausanne a year or two later. This government was confronted with a request to ratify the treaty of Lausanne. If we had accepted the view that our opponents took at the time we would have signed a treaty in the negotiation of which we were not represented, which had not been signed by any representatives of Canada authorized by this government or parliament, p.nd we would have now been committed to the obligations growing out of that treaty. We took the position that not having been asked to participate in the negotiation of that treaty and not having been represented, neither should we be asked to sign the treaty nor this parliament be asked to approve of it, which would be essential for its ratification.
Let me go a step further. This administration in 1926 having these matters in mind,

brought into this house a resolution to the effect that with respect to all treaties in the future, especially those that involved military or economic sanctions, no government of Canada should have the power to commit this country without first bringing the treaties to parliament and having them approved there. I say to my hon. friend that these larger policies are the all-important essential factors in seeking the promotion of peace and international good wiU.
Let me read the last paragraph of a resolution which I introduced into this house on June 21, 1926 and which was subsequently passed. It refers to a resolution of the imperial conference of 1923:
This house approves of the procedure proposed for the negotiation, signature and ratification of treaties and conventions, and considers further that before His Majesty's Canadian ministers advise ratification of a treaty or convention affecting Canada, or signify acceptance of any treaty, convention or agreement involving military or economic sanctions, the approval of the parliament of Canada should be secured.
In other words, our method of promoting peace and international understanding with respect to these very large affairs which come before the nation in its international dealings, is to lay down the doctrine that before this country shall be committed to obligations under a treaty involving military or economic sanctions, that treaty shall first of all be submitted to and approved by this parliament. These are policies that transcend the work of government departments; they reach down to the work of parliament itself.
I may say to my hon, friend that within the last few months the government was asked, with respect to a treaty that was being negotiated between Great Britain and Egypt, whether we would become a party to that treaty. The terms of that treaty are known, they have been published. They involved military sanctions, and they contemplated military alliances. What was the reply of the government to that question? It was that we did not believe that so far as Canada was concerned the parliament of Canada would approve such a course; that if Britain and Egypt could work out a treaty as between themselves along the lines proposed, well and good; but that so far as Canada was concerned, we did not feel that it was in the interests of the British Empire itself or in the interests of the larger peace which it was hoped the treaty would serve, that this country should be asked to become a party to it; and the British government immediately accepted our view in reference thereto.
I say to my hon. friend that questions of international relations have to be considered

International Peace-Mr. Bourassa
more and more as they arise, and depend for their solution, whether from the point of view of peace or from the point of view of war, largely on the view of the administration in office.
May I say this as a last word to my hon. friend: it is because great policies of the kind can be worked out only by administrations that in matters of this nature are strong enough to hold their own, that I appeal so strongly to her and to those about her to see the wisdom of and at all times to realize the importance of having men and women who feel and think alike on these great questions, economic questions and questions of peace and war, so unite their forces that in matters of this kind they may find themselves in the position 'where they will have the final word.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR THE ESTABLISHMENT OF A GOVERNMENT DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to my great regret, I have missed most of this debate. All that I have heard is a part of the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) and the observations of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). With a good deal of the remarks made by the right hon. gentleman I fully agree; but it does not seem to me that he has conclusively answered the object of this motion. As to the inspiration of the policy pursued heretofore by the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues, they are without doubt sincerely peaceful. The right hon. gentleman has a fine record of a peaceful policy ever since he took office, and no doubt what he has gained in the confidence of the people of Canada is largely due to that fact. It is certainly so in the province of Quebec. But the fact that a government has peaceful designs, the fact that an administration has in certain matters of international policy given evidence that it is not prepared to be dragged or to drag the country into war ventures or into dangers of war, does not do away with the position taken by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail).
The Prime Minister is right when he says -and this is nothing new; it has always been that way-that throughout the world there is a current of thought working for peace and a current of thought working for war. The question is: Are governments, and parliaments, and peoples, to take practical, effective means at this time to help the current of peace, in order to counteract the influence for war when the next danger of war comes? This after all is the position. The Prime Minister says that the hon. member for Southeast Grey has minimized the importance of the question. because she suggests the creation of a certain department to promote peace. He
says that all departments of government are interested in preserving peace. But likewise, all departments of government are interested in seeing that the trade of the country is carried on properly. Nevertheless, a department of trade has been created in order to give better assistance to matters of trade and the public interest in trade. The same thing is true in regard to public works, agriculture, labour, and so on. A war department has also been created in the past, and it is still maintained in spite of the peaceful disposition of mind of the government. The Prime Minister thinks there is a strong argument in the fact that the department is called the Department of National Defence. But all the war policies of all countries were prepared under pretence of defence.
The Prime Minister has spoken of the spirit which prevailed prior to the last war. He has vaguely divided the world as between countries bent on war and countries resisting the spirit of war. I think the right hon. gentleman must have known the state of affairs in Europe better than is indicated by his remarks on this point. He should have known -and that was the tragedy of the situation- that in every country in Europe, in Germany as well as France, in Russia as well as Italy, the immense majority of the population, the immense majority of the trading people, the farming people, all people of good will to whatever class they belonged, were opposed to war. But they were led gradually, by the false policies which had been prevalent during the twenty-five years prior to the war, to the conviction, justified or unjustified-I am not passing judgment on that point now-that their country, each of them, was threatened with an attack one of these days, and therefore, that their government was justified in arming the nation to the teeth so as to be prepared to stand the test when war came. It was as true in Germany as in England, in France as in Italy, in Russia as in Austria. But in every one of those countries there were a few people who were bent on war and who worked steadily on two or three factors of war. One of those factors was that sense of fear which Mr. Bertrand Russell so well described during the war as being the mam moral cause which brought most of the countries into the whirlpool. The second was economic rivalry between the various nations. It brought some people in England to this view, for example, as I was told by a high-minded Englishman at the beginning of the war: "We are bent on destroying Germany because she is getting better than us at our own game." Then there was the spirit of national hatred and rivalry which was care-

International Peace-Mr. Bourassa
fully worked on by warmongers, whether they belonged to diplomatic circles, to war organizations or to trade associations. Prejudice was raised in Germany against Russia, in France against Germany, in England against Germany, in Russia against Germany, so that many people of Germany came to have a feeling that they were "encircled" by all the peoples who surrounded them and that their government was justified, nay, was compelled, in taking the first opportunity to strike a blow. I do not say that those suspicions were equally justified. But this was the growing state of mind in Europe, as I could follow it, from time to time, during the fifteen years that preceded the war. I could see the war wave rising steadily in every one of those countries, in England and France as well as in Germany and Italy. It is a falsification of history and popular psychology to pretend that the world was and is divided between nations who want war and nations who want peace. No. There are in every country causes which make for war and causes which make for peace; and it is the highest duty of every government to its own nation and to humanity to take whatever means may be in the hands of political power to strengthen the elements of peace in every country and to minimize the dangers of war. Each country can do that by itself, within itself, and not for its neighbours. We in Canada cannot render either the German, English, Italian or Polish peoples more peaceful than they are; but perhaps we can do something to end here what was done during the war for the purposes of war. Perhaps we can do something to demilitarize or demobilize the minds and souls of the youth of Canada. Perhaps we can accomplish something to develop ideas of peace, to appeal to the highest ideals of humanity as well as to the most selfish interests of any class in this country by demonstrating to them that war is hell, as General Sherman described it, that it is destructive of every moral, social and political principle of order that makes up a nation.
I take the motion presented by the hon. member for Southeast Grey as offering to the government of Canada, responsible as it is for the welfare of the people at large1, an opportunity to help those forces of peace to work for the benefit of the future generations of this country. This generation will probably escape the next war, but if we do not take advantage of the present currents of thought in this country, as elsewhere, to strengthen the forces of peace, the next generation will be caught in the turmoil of war, just as the past generation was caught. Was there any sensible man living in the fall, let us say, of 
1913 in Canada, who imagined that this country would be drawn into the horrors of war within little more than six months? When both parties and all members of parliament appealed to their electors in the previous election, would any single one of them, no matter to what party he belonged, have dared appeal to the people and tell them that in the next parliament, without coming back to the people for a war mandate, they would squander the money of the people of Canada and shed the blood of the youth of Canada in torrents to wage war in Europe? Where is the man, be he Tory or Grit, French or English, who would have dared appeal to the people of Canada during the elections of 1911 upon a war policy? But thanks to the same kind of propaganda to which the right hon. the Prime Minister has referred in connection with the small incident at Chanak, war causes were so manipulated in this country, as well as in every country in Europe for the few months, not to say years, that preceded the war-for many years in Europe, and for several months in Canada-that when the time came, people did not know the real causes of the war, did not know the real causes of rivalry between the two great coalitions in Europe. They simply believed what they were told, and they gave their blood and their treasure-to what purpose? To help one set of nations in Europe get the better of another set, until the next time when the first set, or some new coalition, might have its chance again. That has been the story of Europe for the last four centuries, and so long as the governments in every country in the world do not devote themselves to the work of salvation which the hon. member for Southeast Grey advocates for Canada, it will be the same story over again. Are we going to preserve the' youth of this country from being drawn into the next war as happened to our youth in the last war? Shall we not now take the measures to arouse all the forces of education and enlightenment, and enlist the goodwill of all classes of people, so that when the next time comes, if the government of that day is peacefully disposed, as the Prime Minister is, it will be approved in its refusal to share in the war, or if it is disposed towards war, will be prevented from dragging Canada into the struggle?
The right hon. gentleman has spoken of the work accomplished by his own department. Well and good; but he will permit me, I trust, to tell him that no matter what department of external affairs he may have, no matter what may be the number of the representatives of Canada accredited to gov-

International Peace-Mr. Bourassa
ernments abroad, history should teach him that wars have been made by diplomats even more than by military men. Heaven knows I am anti-militaristic enough; but you must give the devil his due. I really believe that, some acting from a high sense of honour and others from a lower sense of selfishness, military men in the last century have been less responsible for wars and the horrors of war, in which they were mainly the executioners of politicians and diplomats, than those diplomats and politicians themselves. You may have ministers plenipotentiary accredited to all the countries of the world; but if you have not prepared your foreign policy in advance by the proper education of public opinion in your own country, then, when the next crisis comes, when the next time comes to stampede public opinion and the government of this country into a war, your ministers plenipotentiary will be war agenlts, just as some of tlhe ambassadors of Russia and France, of Germany and England were in the ten years which preceded the last war.
With regard to the distinction between war preparation and peace preparation, I must confess that I cannot stop at the point where the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre stopped this evening. Of course I understand his position. He wanted to remain within the precincts of the resolution; but if we are really sincere when we say that we are bent on peace, when we proclaim that we do not want to be dragged into wars in the future, we must here and now, as the right-thinking and the practical-acting pacifists are doing in every other country in the world, reverse the old Roman maxim, Si vis pacem, para bellum; and as Christians who believe in the God of peace, we must at last, after two thousand years of affronted Christianity, proclaim: Si vis pacem, para pacem. Governments should devote at least as much energy and as much propaganda to creating a public opinion in favour of peace as they do to winning an election upon this or that point of fiscal policy or upon the building of a particular branch line of railway. If we are really sincere in our proclamations of the love of peace, we must work for peace, we must organize for peace, and we must create the machinery to help the people who are working for peace.
In the matter of education, the right hon. gentleman has said, and quite properly, that the provincial governments would not like the federal government to impose-I do not think he used that word, but that was the effect -upon them a policy of peaceful education. But did this or any other government stop at the idea of helping provincial governments
in the matter, for instance, of road building? Did it ever stop at helping the provincial governments in promoting health? Health is essentially a matter relating to the person, a matter of concern to the municipal and provincial organizations; and yet we have carried on and are still carrying on propaganda for the maintenance of health, and we are helping the provincial governments in that regard. Why? Because this government is loaded with a national responsibility for the welfare of all the people of Canada. Well, if it is proper for this government to help provincial governments in keeping the people of the various provinces, who are the people of Canada at large, in good health, why should it be improper' for this government to help provincial governments in a propaganda for peace? It is not necessary that schools of peace be established; but if such a department as the hon. member for Southeast Grey suggests were established-not necessarily involving a new portfolio, because I think we are already afflicted with too many of them; I think the Prime Minister and all previous prime ministers have sometimes found the number of portfolios too great, though at certain times they have not enough; and if it were not for the fact that we have so many provinces we could divide the number of our ministers into two and perhaps govern this "huge" country better with six or eight ministers, which would be about the same as they have in the United States with their population of 120,000,000, -why could not the Prime Minister himself, with his peaceful disposition, and with his fine record in the diplomatic world and in inter-imperial relations since 1921, take advantage of the proposal of the hon. member for Southeast Grey and create within his own department a subdepartment for the promotion of peace? That in itself, if advertised to the world, and advertised to the British world first, would have that very effect upon the general tendency of the policies of the various British countries which the Prime Minister's attitude on the Chanak affair had in one single instance. Moreover, magnified as it would necessarily be by the megaphone of the English press, it would reach the League of Nations with a far more potential voice than the simple announcement of the adoption of any policy by our representative there.
Talking of matters of fiscal readjustment, for my part I have lauded, and I repeat my laudation,, the attitude taken by Senator Dandurand when, on the proposals prepared by Sir George Paish for the establishment of fiscal peace, he stated that the government of which he is a member was the first and the

International Peace-Mr. Bourassa
only one since the war that had worked towards the reduction of fiscal tariffs. Likewise, if the government of Canada could announce at the next meeting of the council of the league that it has established, under the direction of the Prime Minister of Canada, in the very department which has to deal with interimperial and external affairs, a special department having for its avowed object, proclaimed by the parliament of Canada, the education of our people in thoughts of peace, of purposes of peace, of policies of peace, it would go a much longer way than the remarks made by the right hon. gentleman that the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture are all peaceable men devoted to works of peace. Of course, everybody knows that. But this would be a new departure and a striking one. You may say that it would be only advertisement and bluff. But we have to take democracies as they are. In the old days, policies, especially international policies, were made by those few men selected from the classes that produced the diplomats of the old school. In those days any definite policy was transmitted from generation to generation, and it developed more or less scientifically in chancelleries and embassies behind closed doors. Now you have to take democracy as it is. It was pretended during the last war that Canada was called upon to shed the blood of five hundred thousand of her sons in order to save democracy. Now that you have made democracy safer than it was before, or otherwise, are you going to take it into your confidence? Are you going to lend the instrument of government to help the democracies of the world save themselves from the ventures imposed upon them by unscrupulous diplomats, by warmongers and by individuals who for the sake of increasing their dividends are prepared to cover the earth with blood, as was done in the last war? Therefore, either from the point of view of national interests or of our inter-British relations-I will not use the word interimperial, because when we talk about peace, the very words, imperial and imperialism, are hateful, and as a matter of fact are contrary to peace-I say, if in the development of our national spirit, in the development of our inter-British relations and in the development of our new-rising relations with the world, we want to make our mark, how can we do it? Shall it be by our great civilization? No; let .us be modest. Shall it be by the development of our artistic work, by the superiority of our literary genius? No; again I say, let us be modest. In this respect we are still at least fifty years behind the

country to the south of us and many centuries behind those great seats of civilization in Europe. But in our primary state of development-a young nation scarcely out of the cradle, but full of resolve to itself and to its future generations in its desire to help the cause of humanity at large-we can modestly but firmly demonstrate that in what we are doing we are working for peace.
The right hon. gentleman has referred to our peaceful relations with the great country to the south of us; and well he did. But I must confess that I am somewhat tired of that theme, for I have heard it so many times in the last fifty years. Why not now make something practical out of it? It has been demonstrated for over a century that a small nation, containing at present no greater population that the cities of New York and Chicago together, could live at peace with its neighbour to the south, the most powerful now of all nations on earth. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has put a very proper question to the Prime Minister. Does the Prime Minister believe that our relations with the United States would be what they are if they had not been absolutely disconnected with any war design or preparation? The question was absolutely accurate, and the answer is obvious. Your International Joint Commission, or any joint body of lawyers or diplomats or engineers, would never have accomplished anything between the two countries if the American government and the American people, with their pride and their democratic spirit of dominance, had thought: Here is a peaceful body, but behind it there is a single fort. The United States have ceased looking upon Canada with a feeling of enmity from the time they first found out that the British government and the British nation, as has been told repeatedly by some of their leading statesmen, would never spend a pound sterling to defend Canada from the United States, and that the people of Canada were courageous enough, as well as modest enough, to take the situation as it was and to deal with their American neighbours in the best manner possible. We have been able to deal fruitfully with the United States since we have demonstrated to the world that we will not and cannot fight against that nation.
Well now, is it not the natural outcome of that long standing lesson, a century old, that we should now tell the world that what we have done in the cause of peace on the North American continent we are prepared to do in maintaining the peace of the world, the pax mundi-first, through our association with

International Peace-Mr. Bourassa
other nations that commune with us in the same principles of government, in establishing peace between ourselves, in imposing, if necessary, a peaceful policy upon the warmongers of London, but also in imposing upon ourselves a peaceful policy in our relations with the rest of the world? It is there that I think my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre remained within the mark.
I have thought over these matters for many years; I have discussed them with some of the most enlightened and thoughtful men of Europe and America, and I have come now to this deep-seated conviction,-that the only manner in which Canada can assure its peace, as far as anything human can be assured, is by disarming totally and absolutely as against the world. There is no powerful country on earth that we could resist with such armed forces as we could muster unless we had help from the United States. I have been taken to task very often for having stated this view, but I may well shelter myself under the authority of every foreign secretary of the king of England for a century past. Every time I have been in London during the last twenty-six years I have interrogated some of the men who had upon their shoulders, or who had had in the past, or would have in the future, the responsibility of peace or war for that great nation; and every one of them without exception, Conservative, Liberal or Labour, has always told me:	"In regard to
the United States there is no change of policy in England; there cannot be; we must rely upon the Monroe doctrine for the preservation of what remains to us of British possessions in America. And far better for you Canadians to realize it."
Secondly, we should take advantage of that situation and proclaim to the world, at Geneva and elsewhere, that when we talk peace we mean peace, when we talk disarmament we are ready to disarm, and when we discuss arbitration we are prepared to arbitrate every time. Let us proclaim to the world that we are determined on every occasion to resort to peaceful arbitration on the principles of justice and equity. It may be contended that this has failed sometimes. Well, it may fail once in a while. But do you suppose that you will secure greater benefits from arbitration and run the risk of war to any less extent by talking peace and at the same time preparing for war, upon however small a scale? Why continue the childish policy of a defence too weak to protect Canada against any conceivable enemy and at the same time just strong enough to inculcate in the national mind, through cadet organizations and through
military training, a military spirit which will be ready to assert itself when the next war breaks out?
I respect the views of all sincere men. I respect the views of those who believe that Canada should participate in all wars in which the empire may be engaged. Such people are imperialists rather than Canadians, but I respect their views just the same. I even respect the views, illogical though they are, of those who style themselves as Canadians and hold that Canada should make herself a close partner in all the quarrels and all the ventures of England, just or unjust, as once was said in this house by the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding. As I say, I respect the opinions of all such people. At the same time I am bound to say I rely more upon the policy which enabled Canada to emerge from that half defined state in which she struggled for so many years previous to confederation-the safe policy that shaped the course of this Dominion in matters relating to Canada and Great Britain on the one hand and Canada and the United States on the other, the policy proclaimed by Macdonald and Cartier at the opening of confederation. And what was that policy? It was this: that for all practical purposes Canada was a neutral country. Some people are scandalised when we speak of Canada's neutrality. But this parliament has erected on the grounds on which this house stands a monument to one of the founders of confederation, D'Arcy McGee, whose motto or, to use a modern Americanism, whose slogan when he appealed to the people of Canada hon. gentlemen may remember. He opposed tooth and nail the militia bill presented in 1862 by the Cartier-Macdonald government, who were defeated on the issue. He said, "If we want to help Canada and the British Empire the only way by which we can do so is to proclaim our neutrality to the world and have it understood not only by British governments but by every foreign country as well." The same principle was propounded in Washington, two or three years ago by Mr. Johnson, the leader of the Labour party in Dublin. And it is the policy which eventually will be accepted.
I had the advantage of meeting in London last year some gentlemen who have much to do in influencing public opinion in England, and they are exceedingly anxious to have this idea generally accepted. Without having the impertinence to make the statement publicly, they desire that the dominions should proclaim their wish to stand neutral in every crisis in which their territory is not directly attacked. Until that time I think we all had been earnestly seeking to find some formula, if I may use the word, through which Canada could express to the world in a sensible and proper way its peaceful desires. Then the Prime Minister introduced, as an illustration of his position, the question of the appointment of Canadian ministers in Tokyo and Paris. That places us at a disadvantage; we are unable to debate that question here, although we intend to debate it later. There are phases of that question which offer room for marked differences of opinion, and I am sorry indeed that it was introduced at all.
I was even more sorry when the Prime Minister raised that controversial question of the Turkish crisis of 1922. He read despatches from British papers, quoting the words of Bonar Law and Lord Asquith, and I think there could have been no other object than to attract to himself in relation to this incident the notice of the world-years later, when we are far removed from the incident and safely past it-and to show that it was he and his decision alone that prevented the outbreak of a new European war. Again that is a subject which might be open to controversy, but I do not wish to enter into a discussion of these subjects to-night.
With the exception of those two references and some of the statements made by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), I find myself very largely in accord with what has been said. However, I wish to say a word or two with regard to some of the suggestions which have been made, particularly looking to the practical side of the question. Eor instance, a good deal of emphasis has been laid upon the desirability of establishing some method or setting up some machinery for educating the people of Canada. The hon. member for Labelle, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, the hon. member for Southeast Grey and others, have laid stress on that point. But I notice that all this emphasizes the fact that public opinion is opposed to war and prone to peace, and would stand by the principles of peace if it were not led astray by its leaders. Now there is no need, to my mind, of educating the people of Canada to peace. We are a peace-loving people to-day. The hon. member for Labelle did give utterance to one very obvious truth, and it was this:	What public man
could go before the people of Canada and

make an appeal on war policy? He would get no support; that is obvious. The people of Canada need no educating in the desirability of peace. And so I would point out that it is not so much the expenditure of public money to educate the people to a sentiment of peace that is required; it is an intelligent direction of our affairs along peaceful lines. The question arises, are we doing that? I rather compliment the Prime Minister upon a large portion of his remarks directed to this end. We have, as a nation, unquestionably directed the general trend of our public administration along peaceful lines. The very fact that for a hundred years we have lived in absolute peace with our neighbours to the south is without doubt one ofthe outstanding illustrations to modern civilization of how two nations can live at peace. Furthermore, to carry on Canada's century-old national trend to deal with international affairs by a process of arbitration is undoubtedly an expression of the genius of the people of this country.
Another suggestion was made that Canada should disarm. I want to call the attention of hon. members .to the fact that Canada is not now armed in the sense that a nation is armed. We ought to keep that clearly in our minds. It is obvious to one who gives a moment's thought to it that we have no armament. On neither of our shores have we any batteries of artillery. We have a couple of small ships that serve for little'more than coastguard vessels; I doubt if they can effectively carry out that purpose. Our forces are insignifioant. But we must also bear in mind that just so long as there are people in the community who will resist the law, any government-it matters not what government it is or what its stripe may be-must have some arm or force or power, call it police force if you like, to enforce its laws. Whether that is done by a police force or with the support of a very moderate militia establishment does not make very much difference, but you must have some support of that character. I will deal in a moment with the theoretical side of the question.
The hon. member for AVinnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) suggested that we should promote an exchange of students. I direct the attention of the house to the fact that we are carrying on that work now, and carrying it on very effectively. Canada does exchange students with France and with Great Britain-I do not know whether we do so with other countries, but we certainly do with those two-and in that respect we are carrying on a very useful work.

The hon. member pointed out that science and art had overleaped, as he said, international boundaries and' were themselves international. Certainly they are-so is commerce and so is finance. It is because of the establishment of a growing confidence between nation and nation that these things are becoming more and more international rather than matters limited and peculiar to various nations. And so the great cause of peace, if you like to call it that, is progressing. Progressing how? Progressing along lines established by commerce, by art, by science, and I hope and trust-in fact I am sure-by a moral sense of responsibility, among nations, and among men, which is underlying it all.
It seems to me that we have lost sight of one thought:	Peace will never be brought
about by propaganda. Take the member for Labelle-and I am sorry that he has left his seat. It would be a considerable time before he and I couldi agree upon some line of propaganda for a peace society or a peace department for Canada. I submit that it is an impracticable thing. I could not agree with his premises; he would not agree with mine. It is not so much a question of education or propaganda. Peace is based upon a will for peace, just as war comes out df a will for war. This country is not saturated or impregnated with a desire for or rather a will for war. Our people of all classes have absolutely the will for peace, and as long as we can give expression to that in our legislation, in our administration, in our public sentiment, so long shall we promote the cause of peace.
One other thought, sir, and then I take my seat. You will never bring about peace- and I say this with the greatest of sincerity and with the utmost reverence, not in any sense for the sake of show but rather from a deep conviction of its truth-you will never get peace in this world by philosophical dissertations about it, by propaganda. There is only one method I know of and that is by promoting the principles of the Prince of Peace; that is the way in which peace will be brought to the world. And while undoubtedly we are very often guilty of a disregard of these great and sacred principles, I find there is a great conflict in my own mind, and I know there is in the mind and the heart of almost every man and woman I meet, in endeavouring to reconcile these principles of peace with the problems of everyday life. It is very easy and veiy simple to give utterance to platitudinous arguments and expressions about peace, but it is a very different thing to harmonize these ideas with one's
